必無獸心雖有獸心以狀而見親矣傳冀戴角分牙布爪仰飛伏走謂之禽獸未必無人心雖有人心以狀而見疏矣庖犧氏女媧氏神農氏夏后氏蛇身人面牛首虎鼻此有非人之狀而有大聖之德夏桀殷紂魯桓楚穆狀貌七竅皆同於人而有禽獸之心而眾人守一狀以求至智未可幾也黃帝與炎帝戰於阪泉之野帥熊羆狼豹豼貅虎為前驅雕鶡鷹鳶為旗幟此以力使禽獸者也堯使夔典樂擊石拊石百獸率舞簫韶九成鳳凰來儀

<margin>兩此意可</margin>
<margin>列子 黃帝</margin>

But it does not follow that a man may not have the mind of a brute. Even though this be the case, other men will still recognise him as one of their own species in virtue of his outward form. Creatures which have wings on the back or horns on the head, serrated teeth or extensile talons, which fly overhead or run on all fours, are called birds and beasts. But it does not follow that a bird or a beast may not have the mind of a man. Yet, even if this be so, it is nevertheless assigned to another species because of the difference in form. P'ao Hsi, Nü Kua, Shen Nung and Hsia Hou had serpents' bodies, human faces, ox-heads and tigers' snouts. Thus, their forms were not human, yet their virtue was of the saintliest. Chieh of the Hsia dynasty, Chou of the Yin, Huan of the Lu State, and Mu of the Ch'u State, were in all external respects, as facial appearance and possession of the seven channels of sense, like unto other men; yet they had the minds of savage brutes. Howbeit, in seeking perfect wisdom, men attend to the outward form alone, which will not bring them near to it.

When the Yellow Emperor fought with Yen Ti on the field of P'an-ch'uan, his vanguard was composed of bears, wolves, panthers, lynxes and tigers, while his ensign-bearers were eagles, ospreys, falcons and kites. This was forcible impressment of animals into the service of man. The Emperor Yao entrusted K'uei with the regulation of music. When the latter tapped the musical stone in varying cadence, all the animals danced to the sound of the music. When the strains of the Shao were heard on the flute, the phoenix itself flew down to assist.

<meta>The text continues a discourse on the nature of internal character versus outward appearance, arguing that physical form does not dictate one's humanity or virtue.</meta>

<margin>Both these points are acceptable</margin>
<margin>Liezi, Yellow Emperor</margin>

One may lack the heart of a beast, yet because of one's appearance, one is treated with the closeness reserved for one's own kind. The traditions state that those with horns, teeth, claws, who fly, walk, crouch, or run are called birds and beasts. They do not necessarily lack the heart of a human, yet because of their appearance, they are treated with alienation. Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, and the sovereigns of the Xia dynasty had bodies like snakes, human faces, ox heads, and tiger noses. They possessed forms that were not human, yet they held the virtues of the great sages. Jie of Xia, Zhou of Shang, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu all possessed the features and seven orifices exactly the same as any human, yet they harbored the hearts of beasts. For the common people to rely solely on outward appearance to seek supreme wisdom is to remain far from the truth. The Yellow Emperor fought the Flame Emperor on the plains of Banquan. He commanded bears, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>mythical fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, while eagles, falcons, and kites served as his banners. This was a case of using strength to command birds and beasts. When Yao appointed Kui to oversee music, striking stones and beating percussion instruments, a hundred beasts danced in sequence. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>a legendary ancient musical composition</gloss> was played in nine movements, the phoenix came to perform its rites.

<summary>This passage contrasts external appearance with internal moral character, citing mythological sage-kings with non-human features alongside tyrannical rulers with human forms to argue that human nature is defined by virtue rather than physical shape.</summary>

If one possesses no animal heart, even if they have an animal-like appearance, they are still regarded with intimacy. Legends tell of creatures with horns, fangs, and claws that fly, soar, crouch, and run, yet are called birds and beasts. If one possesses a human heart, even if they have a human appearance, they are still regarded with alienation. Fuxi, Nüwa, Shennong, and the sovereigns of the Xia dynasty had the bodies of snakes and human faces, or ox heads and tiger noses. These had appearances that were not human, yet they possessed the virtues of great sages. Jie of Xia, Zhou of Shang, Huan of Lu, and Mu of Chu all possessed human appearances and features, yet they had the hearts of birds and beasts. The common people focus only on outward appearances to judge wisdom, which is hardly a way to approach the truth. When the Yellow Emperor fought the Flame Emperor on the plains of Banquan, he led bears, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>mythical fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his vanguard, and used eagles, falcons, and kites as his flags and banners. These are those who used their power to command birds and beasts. When Yao appointed Kui to oversee music, he struck the stones and beat the chimes, and all the beasts danced in accordance. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>a legendary ancient musical composition</gloss> was performed in nine movements, the phoenixes came to present their grace.

translations.T4:
<meta>The text continues the philosophical exploration of the distinction between physical form and inner nature, specifically focusing on the "Yellow Emperor" chapter of the Liezi.</meta>

If they lack the heart of a beast, even if they possess the physical form of a beast, they will be treated with kinship because of their nature. On the other hand, those who are described as having horns, divided teeth, spread claws, those who fly above or crawl below, are called birds and beasts <note>original: 禽獸 <term>qinshou</term></note>; yet they do not necessarily lack a human heart. Although some possess a human heart, they are treated with distance because of their physical appearance. 

<term>Paoxi</term> <gloss>Fuxi</gloss>, <term>Nuwa</term>, <term>Shennong</term>, and the Lord of Xia <note>Yu the Great</note> had bodies like snakes, faces like humans, heads like oxen, or noses like tigers. These figures had appearances that were not human, yet they possessed the virtue of great sages. In contrast, <term>Jie</term> of Xia, <term>Zhou</term> of Yin, <term>Huan</term> of Lu, and <term>Mu</term> of Chu all had appearances and sensory organs <note>the seven apertures of the head</note> identical to other humans, yet they possessed the hearts of birds and beasts. If the common people rely solely on physical appearance to seek supreme wisdom, they will never come close to finding it.

<margin>These two points are acceptable.</margin>
<margin>Liezi: Yellow Emperor.</margin>

The <term>Huangdi</term> <gloss>Yellow Emperor</gloss> fought against <term>Yandi</term> <gloss>the Flame Emperor</gloss> in the wilderness of <term>Banquan</term>. He led bears, grizzly bears, wolves, leopards, <term>pixiu</term> <gloss>fabulous fierce beasts</gloss>, and tigers as his forward scouts, while eagles, black eagles, falcons, and kites served as his banners. This is an example of using power to command birds and beasts. <term>Yao</term> appointed <term>Kui</term> to oversee music. When the stone chimes were struck and patted, all the beasts were led to dance. When the <term>Xiaoshao</term> <gloss>the music of Shun</gloss> was played nine times, the <term>fenghuang</term> <gloss>phoenixes</gloss> came to pay court.

<summary>This page argues that true nature is independent of physical form, citing sages with animal features and tyrants with human features. It also describes legendary rulers like the Yellow Emperor and Yao who could command and harmonize with animals.</summary>
